records.place: Minies, near Argostoli, PDO Robola of Cephalonia, Kefalonia, Ionian Islands, Greece

wine.name: Gentilini Robola Wild Paths
wine.grapes: Robola alone, the white grape of the island's appellation.
wine.sites: A single vineyard, the house's oldest, of ungrafted bush vines at about 850 metres on poor, rocky limestone on the slopes of Mount Ainos, inside the Robola zone.
wine.making: The free run juice is split in two: half is fermented with a commercial yeast and half with a native Robola yeast the house isolated itself. About a fifth of the wine spends time in French and American oak barrels, and the lots are blended after four months of stirring on the lees, by the house's own sheet.
wine.glass: Lemon, citron and white peach over a flinty, stony edge, with a touch of vanilla from the barrels, fresh acidity and a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Open on release, it gains breadth and a honeyed note over three or four years, as Robola tends to do by the national wine body's account.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass with some room for the oak.

label.means: The island's protected designation of origin for dry white Robola, set up in 1982.
The house's name for its single vineyard Robola, half fermented with a native yeast.
Protected Designation of Origin: the appellation, with its own zone and its own rules.

records.table: High on the limestone of Mount Ainos, the oldest vineyard of the house gives Gentilini Robola Wild Paths, half fermented with the house's native yeast and a little of it in oak. Lemon, citron and white peach run over flint; it wants grilled fish.
records.story: The name comes from the island's Venetian past: a military engineer of the Gentilini family was commissioned by the Venetian Senate to build the fortifications of Assos in 1593, and the name passed down to the family of the founder, as the house tells it. The founder came back to Kefalonia from abroad and, by the house's account, planted his first plot of an obscure local white grape, Robola, in 1978. The first small vintage, of 1984, was released in Athens and London at once, and Gentilini became one of the first modern estates of the island, by the guides' account. The appellation of Robola of Cephalonia had been set up only two years before, in 1982, on the Omala plateau and the slopes of Mount Ainos. In 2002 the founder's daughter and her husband took the estate on as its second generation. Their Wild Paths is a single vineyard Robola from the oldest vines, at about 850 metres, half fermented with a yeast the house isolated from its own Robola, while the older Robola Cellar Selection, sold into the early 2010s, is no longer in the house's range. Altitude, limestone and a little oak: Wild Paths shows how much depth Robola can gain from the three.

others.name: Gentilini Robola
others.note: The house's classic Robola of Cephalonia, from its vineyards on Mount Ainos inside the zone.

others.name: Gentilini Rhombus Robola
others.note: A second Robola of Cephalonia in the range.

traps: Robola of Cephalonia is a Greek appellation for the Robola grape; it is not the Ribolla Gialla of Friuli, whatever the likeness of the names.
Wild Paths is not wholly wild fermented: half the juice ferments with a commercial yeast and half with the house's own native yeast.

cards.front: Gentilini Wild Paths: how is the fermentation split?
cards.back: Half with a commercial yeast and half with a native Robola yeast the house isolated; about a fifth sees oak.

cards.front: In what year did Gentilini release its first small vintage, and where?
cards.back: 1984, released in Athens and London at once.

questions.q: A guest asks where the grapes for Gentilini Robola Wild Paths grow. Which reply fits?

Sandy vineyards by the sea at Minies
Bought fruit from the Paliki peninsula
Clay vineyards on the Omala plateau floor
questions.exp: Wild Paths is a single vineyard Robola from the house's oldest vines, high on rocky limestone; the winery stands near the coast at Minies, but this fruit grows far higher.

questions.q: Gentilini takes its name from a family of Kefalonia's past. What story does the house tell of it?
opts: A Venetian engineer who fortified Assos in 1593
A British governor of the Ionian protectorate
A monk of the monastery of Saint Gerasimos
A shipowner who traded wheat from Odessa
questions.exp: The house traces the name to a Gentilini engineer commissioned by the Venetian Senate to build the Assos fortifications in 1593; the Odessa shipowners belong to the Sclavos story.

report: SWAP PROPOSED: the plan's Robola Cellar Selection is not on the house's site or in any current listing found; the house's single vineyard flagship is Robola Wild Paths, so the pick's wine should become Robola Wild Paths.

The wine name carries the old words only so the record lints against the plan; that Wild Paths succeeded the Cellar Selection rests on one guide's summary and the plan's own note, so a refuter should confirm it or cut the clause from the name and the story.

The plan places the Cellar Selection on the Fagias vineyard; no source ties Fagia to Gentilini, while a shop's sheet names a pre phylloxera vineyard of Fagia as a source of a Petrakopoulos Robola, so Fagia is left out here.
Founded is 1984, the first vintage by the house and two guides; the house's first planting was 1978, and two guides put the founder's first interest in the 1960s, which is left out.
The founder and his heirs are living or undated, so nobody of the family is named; the engineer of 1593 has no dates in any source, so he is described, not named.
The house's pages differ on whether the fifth in oak is fermented or only aged there, so the record says it spends time in oak; volumes and scores are left out.
Searches for this record: six of the group's 35; no fetch tried.

changed: wine.sites: ungrafted bush vines added, by the house's Wild Paths page and its technical sheet of 2019.

story: was that Wild Paths took the place of the Cellar Selection at the head of the range, on one guide; now the older Robola Cellar Selection is told as sold into the early 2010s (Falstaff's 2010 and CellarTracker's 2012 listings) and no longer in the range, with no claim that one succeeded the other.
others: the classic Robola was said to be made in steel with weeks of lees stirring, unsourced; now from the house's vineyards on Mount Ainos inside the zone, by the house's Robola page.
open: The wine name still carries the words once the Robola Cellar Selection only so it lints against the plan; when the read-together agent applies the swap to Robola Wild Paths, the name becomes Robola Wild Paths alone.
Founded 1984 is the first vintage; a trade catalogue gives 1978, the first planting, as the founding. The record keeps 1984 and tells 1978 in the story.
Botilia names the 850 metre vineyard as Fagia; the house's own pages do not, so Fagia stays out for want of a second source.

records.place: Kechrion, near Lixouri, Paliki peninsula, Kefalonia, Ionian Islands, Greece

wine.name: Vino di Sasso
wine.sites: Vines of about thirty years in the Robola zone at about 650 to 700 metres, on broken limestone under Mount Ainos, by the house's account.
wine.making: The house describes its making as biodynamic: a long extraction, then alcoholic and malolactic fermentation both completed with the grapes' own native yeasts, so that little stands between the stony site and the glass.
wine.glass: Pear and lemon over wet stone and a saline edge, bone dry, with taut acidity; riper and broader in a warm year, with more texture as it ages.
wine.ageing: Taut and stony on release, it is made to keep for two or three years, gaining texture as it goes.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: Wine of the stone, an old Italian name for Robola from the island's limestone.
The island's protected designation of origin for dry white Robola.
Protected Designation of Origin: the appellation, with its own zone and its own rules.

records.table: Sclavos Vino di Sasso is a Robola from high limestone on Mount Ainos, fermented through malolactic with its own native yeasts. The name means wine of the stone, and the glass bears it out: pear, lemon and wet stone, bone dry.
records.story: The Sclavos family were shipowners from Livatho, in the south of Kefalonia, and by the house's account a branch of the family traded from Odessa on the Black Sea, where around 1860 a great grandfather of the present winemaker ran a large wine business that the family owned. The Russian revolution of 1917 ended that life, and in 1919 the grandfather came home and planted the first vines on the family's land at Kechrion, on the Paliki peninsula below Laskaratos Hill. In the 1990s, two generations on, the family remade the old vineyard and turned to organic and then biodynamic farming, and the family's own vines came to be certified by Demeter. The name, wine of the stone, is an old one for Robola: the house credits it to a British official of the island in the years of British rule, while a Greek guide gives it to the Venetians, and both agree it speaks of the limestone in the glass. Vino di Sasso is Robola made with as light a hand as the family can manage, and its very name a reminder that the island's names carry Italian as well as Greek.

others.name: Sclavos Metagitnion
others.note: A white of Vostilidi, one of the island's rare local grapes, from old vines on their own roots at Kechrion, by the house's account.

others.name: Sclavos Orgion
others.note: A Mavrodaphne of Cephalonia, the island's red grape, from the family's vineyards.

traps: Vino di Sasso is the wine's name, not an Italian appellation: the label's appellation is PDO Robola of Cephalonia.
The family's home vineyard at Kechrion lies on the Paliki peninsula, while Robola of Cephalonia comes from the Robola zone on the slopes of Mount Ainos.

cards.front: Sclavos: what does the name Vino di Sasso mean?

cards.front: In what year did the Sclavos grandfather return from Odessa and plant vines on Kefalonia?
cards.back: 1919, at Kechrion on the Paliki peninsula, after the Russian revolution.

questions.q: A guest asks how Sclavos ferments its Vino di Sasso. Which reply fits the house's own account?
opts: With native yeasts, through the malolactic
With a cultured yeast, in new oak
Halted early to keep sweetness
With carbonic maceration of whole bunches
questions.exp: The house completes both the alcoholic and the malolactic fermentation with the grapes' own native yeasts after a long extraction; the wine is bone dry, so no fermentation is halted for sweetness.

questions.q: Before the Sclavos family planted on Kefalonia in 1919, where did a branch of it run a family wine business?
opts: Odessa, on the Black Sea
Venice, on the Adriatic
Alexandria, in Egypt
Trieste, under Austrian rule
questions.exp: By the house's account a branch of the family traded from Odessa, and around 1860 a great grandfather ran a large family wine business there; Venice is the island's older past, not this family's.

The house's About page dates the remaking of the vineyard to 1990, while the Greek Gastronomy Guide, which draws on the house, gives 1995; the record keeps the house's 1990.

The origin of the name Vino di Sasso differs: the house credits a British official it names as Napier, the guide credits the Venetians; both are told, and Napier is not named because his dates were not checked in two sources.
The year of the biodynamic certification was not found, so none is given; the Demeter mark rests on the house's product page and a retailer.
The tasting note rests on importers' sheets and a critic's note whose address names a living writer, which is not cited; the smoky edge of the region record is not repeated, for want of a source.
The living winemaker and his father are not named; the grandfather and great grandfather have no dates in any source and are described.
Searches for this record: six of the group's 35; no fetch tried.

story: was the vineyard remade from 1990 with Mavrodaphne and Vostilidi planted and among the first biodynamic estates in Greece; the house gives 1990 and the guide 1995, and the house's own Vostilidi comes from vines of more than ninety years; now the vineyard remade in the 1990s, organic then biodynamic farming, the family's own vines certified by Demeter, with no claim of a first.

others: Sclavos Vostilidi and Sclavos Mavrodaphne are not label names; now Metagitnion, the house's Vostilidi from old ungrafted vines (sclavoswines.gr), and Orgion, its Mavrodaphne of Cephalonia (Cream Wine Company, Shrine to the Vine).
cards: the name card now says the house credits the name to a British official, as the story tells it.

The Napier of the house's account is not named: the house does not give his full name, and the likely Charles James Napier was not confirmed as the man it means.

records.place: Omala valley, PDO Robola of Cephalonia, Kefalonia, Ionian Islands, Greece

wine.name: Orealios Gaea Robola of Cephalonia
wine.sites: Members' vineyards across the Robola zone, on the Omala plateau and the western slopes of Mount Ainos, between about 175 and 800 metres, many of them old, low trained goblet vines on limestone.
wine.making: Robola oxidises easily, so, as the national wine body describes the island's way with it, it is made with care to keep it from the air and is normally fermented and kept entirely in stainless steel tanks, cool, before an early bottling.
wine.glass: Delicate lemon with a touch of salt and wet stone, medium in body and lifted by the high acidity of the grape, with a clean finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young and fresh; a good vintage rounds out over three or four years, turning mineral and faintly honeyed.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; there is no call to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The island's protected designation of origin for dry white Robola, set up in 1982.
The trading name of the Robola co-operative of Kefalonia, whose growers own it.
Protected Designation of Origin: the appellation, with its own zone and its own rules.

records.table: The island's growers' co-operative gathers the greater part of Kefalonia's Robola, and Orealios Gaea Robola of Cephalonia, from the Omala plateau and the slopes of Mount Ainos, is made in steel. Lemony and salty, it is the plain glass to pour cold with fish.
records.story: About three hundred of the island's growers founded the Robola co-operative of Kefalonia in 1982, the same year in which the appellation of Robola of Cephalonia was set up, as the national wine body records both. The zone lies in the south of the island, on the Omala plateau and the western and northwestern slopes of Mount Ainos, and its slopes hold many old vines on their own roots. In 1987 the co-operative's own winery was completed with state help, beside the monastery of Saint Gerasimos, the island's patron saint, by two guides' accounts. It trades as Orealios Gaea, and by the national wine body's account it gathers the greater part of the island's Robola grapes, which makes its bottling the one a server is most likely to meet. In 2005 it renewed its cellar equipment and added a unit to treat its waste water. Beside the plain Robola it makes San Gerasimo, named for the saint, from higher, semi mountain vineyards. The grape, the limestone and the island's growers, without oak or artifice: the co-operative's Robola is the appellation stated plainly.

others.name: San Gerasimo
others.note: The co-operative's selection of Robola of Cephalonia from higher, semi mountain vineyards, chosen in the vineyard year by year.

traps: Orealios Gaea is the trading name of the Robola co-operative of Kefalonia, not a separate family estate.
Robola of Cephalonia is a dry white only; the island's sweet wines are Mavrodaphne of Cephalonia and Muscat of Cephalonia.

cards.front: Orealios Gaea: what is it, and when was it founded?
cards.back: The Robola co-operative of Kefalonia, founded by about three hundred of the island's growers in 1982.

cards.front: What came to the Robola co-operative of Kefalonia, Orealios Gaea, in 1987?
cards.back: Its own winery, completed with state help beside the monastery of Saint Gerasimos.

questions.q: A guest asks how Orealios Gaea Robola of Cephalonia is made. Which reply fits the island's way of making it?

In new French oak barriques
In clay amphorae buried in the ground
On its skins for weeks, as an orange wine
questions.exp: Robola oxidises easily, so it is normally made entirely in stainless steel; new barriques and long skin contact are other styles, never this co-operative bottling.

questions.q: The Robola co-operative of Kefalonia and the appellation of Robola of Cephalonia share a founding year. Which year?
questions.exp: Both date from 1982 by the national wine body's record; 1987 is the year the co-operative's own winery was completed and 2005 the year it renewed its equipment.

report: The 1982 founding and the 1982 appellation are both on the Wines of Greece pages, a national wine body; 1987 rests on two guides and 2005 on the national body alone.

The co-operative's own site was not found, so the making and the tasting note of the plain Robola are drawn from the national body's account of the variety and the island's way with it, not from a sheet of this wine; a refuter may wish to find one.

The guides differ on the winery's height (410 metres in one, a plateau at 700 metres in the other), so no height is given for the winery; the share of the island's grapes (about 85 per cent in one source, 70 in another) is volatile and left as the greater part.
The region record speaks of lemon, flint and smoke in Robola; the national wine body speaks of delicate citrus and salinity, and the record follows the body.
San Gerasimo's first release of 1995 rests on a writer's site whose address names a living person, so it is not given.
Searches for this record: six of the group's 35; no fetch tried.

wine.name: Hariton Vostilidi
wine.grapes: Vostilidi alone, a rare white grape of Kefalonia that has come back into the island's vineyards.
wine.sites: The family's organically farmed vineyard around the farmhouse of 1863 at Kladata, near Lixouri on the Paliki peninsula.
wine.making: Made dry and without barrique, by a shop's technical sheet, and bottled at the estate, by the house's account; the house publishes no fuller account of the cellar, so this record gives none.
wine.glass: Bergamot, lime, lemon and peach over melon, with jasmine and orange blossom, a salty edge, an oily texture and crisp acidity through a medium body.
wine.ageing: Fresh on release; a shop's sheet gives it about three years, and its texture grows in that time.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decanting is not needed; a white wine glass.

label.means: The wine's name, a tribute to the family's grandfather.
The grape, a rare white of Kefalonia, spelt Vostylidi by the house.
A regional indication of Kefalonia, wider than the Robola appellation and open to other grapes.

records.table: Pure Vostilidi, a rare white grape of Kefalonia, makes Haritatos Hariton, from the family's organic vineyard at Kladata on the Paliki peninsula. Bergamot, lime and orange blossom lie over an oily, salty texture, good company for seafood or a tartare.
records.story: The family was once known by the fuller name Typaldos Haritatos, as the house tells it, and the estate at Kladata, near Lixouri on the Paliki peninsula, took its present shape in 1863, the year of the stone farmhouse at its heart; the vineyard has stayed in the family ever since. Around the farmhouse stand a family chapel, olive groves, medicinal plants and the vines. The house grows Mavrodaphne and has brought back Vostilidi, a white grape of Kefalonia that had almost slipped from its vineyards. Because the Robola of Cephalonia appellation, dating from 1982, admits only Robola, the family's Vostilidi is labelled under the wider regional indication of the Slopes of Aenos. Hariton, named in tribute to the family's grandfather, is pure Vostilidi, and the house calls it perhaps the first wine of the grape alone bottled for sale. The vineyard is farmed organically and the wines are bottled at the estate. When a guest asks what Kefalonia grows besides Robola, Hariton is the answer, from a family whose land has not changed hands since 1863.

others.name: Mademoiselle Haritatou
others.note: The family's dry red of Mavrodaphne, the island's red grape.

others.name: Typaldo
others.note: A white whose name recalls the family's older name, Typaldos Haritatos, by the house's account.

traps: Vostilidi is not Robola: a Vostilidi cannot carry the Robola of Cephalonia appellation, so Hariton is labelled PGI Slopes of Aenos.
Haritatos is a family estate at Kladata on the Paliki peninsula, not the Robola co-operative of the Omala valley.

It is a sweet wine, which the appellation forbids
It is aged in oak, which the appellation forbids
Its vineyard lies on the mainland
questions.exp: Robola of Cephalonia admits only Robola, so a pure Vostilidi takes the wider regional indication; Hariton is dry and its vineyard is on Kefalonia's Paliki peninsula.

report: The plan's flagship, Vostilidi, is the house's Hariton, a pure Vostilidi; the wine name keeps the plan's word, so no swap is needed, though a refuter may prefer the plan to read Hariton.
Founded is left empty: 1863 is the farmhouse and the vineyard's present shape, not a winery's founding, and a family member gives 1860 for the cottage; no first vintage of Hariton was found.

PGI Slopes of Aenos rests on an importer and a shop; the grandfather's tribute on the same two; the tank fermentation and four months on lees in one importer's sheet are left out for want of a second source.

The house's claim that Hariton is perhaps the first pure Vostilidi bottled for sale is told as its claim; Typaldo's grape is left unsaid, since one listing calls it a Muscat and its name ties it to the ancestor only by the house.
The three siblings who run the estate are living and not named, nor is the Venetian ancestor, whom no source dates.
Volumes and the estate's size differ between sources and are left out as volatile.

wine.name: Melissinos Natural Robola
wine.sites: Organically farmed Robola on terraces around the winery at Thiramonas, below Mount Ainos, and from other vineyards in the Robola zone.
wine.making: Made from organically farmed Robola with as little intervention as the house can manage, which is what the word Natural on its label promises; the house publishes no fuller account of the cellar, so this record gives none.
wine.glass: Lemon and wild herbs over a stony, saline line, wilder and more savoury than a plain Robola, with the grape's high, fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Open young; like other Robola it can fill out and turn towards honey in three or four years.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: The house's word for Robola made with as little intervention as it can manage.
The island's protected designation of origin for dry white Robola.

records.table: Little is done in the cellar to Melissinos Natural Robola, made from organic vines at a small winery at Thiramonas, below Mount Ainos. Wilder and more herbal than most Robola, it suits wild greens as well as fish.
records.story: Thiramonas is a village of south Kefalonia, set below Mount Ainos, the mountain whose western slopes hold much of the Robola zone, the appellation of 1982. The winery began in 2002 beside the family's old house in the village, by two guides' accounts, working in small lots and only with the island's own grapes, Robola, Mavrodaphne and Zakynthino among them. Its first name, Melissinos, is an old family name of the island, from which the founder descends by one guide's account. The vineyard around the winery is farmed organically, its Robola planted on terraces. The house's Natural Robola, bottled under the Melissinos name in the middle of the 2010s, drew notice in the foreign press as a wilder, more herbal Robola than most, made with very little done in the cellar. Later vintages carry the family's other name, Petrakopoulos, and the Natural Robola appears as Robola Natural Palia Armakia, so a guest may meet one wine under two houses' names. The Natural Robola shows the appellation's quieter, low intervention side, from a small family winery of the island's south.

others.name: Palia Armakia
others.note: A natural Robola of Cephalonia released under the Petrakopoulos name.

others.name: Thymari Petras
others.note: A single vineyard Robola from the Lakkomatia hillside at about 600 metres, named for the thyme among the vines.

traps: Melissinos and Petrakopoulos are one winery at Thiramonas under two names, not two houses.
Natural on this label is the house's word for low intervention, not a legal category of the Robola appellation.

cards.front: Melissinos Natural Robola: at which village is the winery?
cards.back: Thiramonas, in south Kefalonia, below Mount Ainos.

cards.front: Under what other name do later vintages of the Melissinos winery appear?
cards.back: Petrakopoulos, the family's other name, with the natural Robola labelled Palia Armakia.

questions.q: A guest sees the word Natural on a bottle of Melissinos Robola. What does it tell them?

A legal rank of the appellation
A wine with no alcohol in it
A blend of Robola with Zakynthino
questions.exp: Natural is the house's word for a low intervention Robola from organic vines; the appellation has no such rank, and the wine is Robola alone.

questions.q: In what year did the winery at Thiramonas, first known as Melissinos, begin to make wine?
questions.exp: Two guides date the winery's start to 2002; 1982 is the Robola appellation and 1987 the co-operative's winery.

sources.title: Monocle: Kefalonia, a Greek wine renaissance
Wines of Greece: PDO Robola of Kefalonia

report: SWAP PROPOSED: the winery first known as Melissinos trades as Petrakopoulos by Decanter, two shops and a guide, and its Natural Robola is labelled Palia Armakia or Orina Armakia; the pick should become Petrakopoulos with Palia Armakia, or give way to Sarris, a Lixouri house with a Robola and the V for Vostilidi.
No house page was found, so the record has no primary source of its own; every fact rests on two of the guides, shops and magazines cited, and the year of the renaming was not found.
Founded is 2002, the start of winemaking by two guides; the descent from the Melissinos family rests on one guide and is hedged.

The making is thin on purpose: spontaneous fermentation, the share of sulphur and stainless steel each rest on one source, one of them a writer's site whose address names a living person, and are left out.
The plan's fir trees of the National Park rest on one magazine and are left out; Orina Armakia's vineyards (Lakomatia, Troianata and Fagia) rest on one shop and are left out.
The founders, two brothers, are living and not named.
Searches for this record: four of the group's 35, with two searches on the appellation shared across the group; no fetch tried.

changed: story, card: the natural Robola was said to appear as Palia Armakia and Orina Armakia; only Palia Armakia is labelled Robola Natural (Botilia, Greece and Grapes), so Orina Armakia is cut.
others: Thymari Petras now from the Lakkomatia hillside at about 600 metres, named for the thyme among the vines (Botilia and a second listing).
open: The swap to Petrakopoulos with Robola Natural Palia Armakia is accepted; the read-together agent applies it to plan.json, with a new key, and then the producer, the wine name and the say of this record follow it.
Spontaneous fermentation with little sulphur rests on one shop and a critic's site naming a living writer, so the making stays thin.
